text.content: 13: Threats very mission gets complicated. Every adventure has twists and turns. Strange phenomena, harsh environments, and ruthless adversaries can be found throughout The Expanse and are key when designing campaigns as a Game Master. This chapter provides the tools to create threats for your heroes to face, divided into two categories: Hazards and Adversaries.

The galaxy is full of dangers that have nothing to do with staring down the barrel of a gun or outmaneuvering an OPA raider at high-g. Characters might contend with “How many times can you get yourself massively fire, the vacuum of space, sudden falls or impacts, and a host of other everyday irradiated before it catches up with you?”

“At least once more?”

The AGE System handles hazards with a simple set of questions used to simulate everything from a sudden hull breach to a toxic alien environment. Adventures Caliban’s War will provide specific hazards for your players, but when you need to adjudicate one on your own, answer the following questions.

WHAT IS THE NATURE OF THE HAZARD?

Describe the hazard in a general way. It could be a small fire in a ship’s galley, a pressure plate attached to a string of explosives, or the rumble of a groundside earthquake.

CAN IT BE AVOIDED?

Some hazards, such as traps, are hidden. A Perception test with an appropriate focus might detect them; for example, a PC could use Seeing to notice a path of disturbed earth over a buried landmine. If there is a chance of detection, set the TN for the ability test as usual. PCs who make a successful test can avoid the hazard or at least get a clue to help them do so. Those that fail walk right into it.

You also need to decide if armor protects against the hazard. If it does not, the hazard inflicts penetrating damage. Common sense should dictate whether armor helps in each situation. For example, someone wearing Martian power armor would be protected against the galley fire.

DOES IT HAVE ANY SPECIAL EFFECTS?

Some hazards do more than inflict damage. For example, they might impose a temporary penalty to ability tests or Speed. In many cases, these special effects can be handled with conditions (see Conditions in the Player’s Section). Try to remember that a character’s health is an abstract in the first place, so many hazards require no special effects.

HOW LONG DOES IT LAST?

Many hazards happen once and then end. For example, a string of explosives detonates once when triggered. Other hazards can be ongoing. Characters running through a dust storm on an alien world might take damage each round until they find cover. Again, use common sense as your guide to determine whether the hazard is a single incident or reoccurring.

Heroes in The Expanse can encounter any number of hazards that might harm or even kill them. This section outlines several that follow the guidelines presented previously. You can modify or use these as templates to create your own in-game hazards. Additional hazards will appear in future adventures and supplemental material.

Acceleration

High-g acceleration has a punishing effect on human biology. The effective substantial increase in weight can cause fainting and bruising as blood pools or is pushed “downward.” More severely, acceleration can cause difficulty breathing, organ failure, stroke, or cardiac arrest. This usually involves a measure of damage based on the intensity of the acceleration; a drug cocktail known as “the juice” (see Chapter 4) helps mitigate this and keep crew members conscious and able to function under high acceleration. In action scenes, harm from acceleration usually occurs as the result of ship maneuvers (see Space Combat in Chapter 6). Characters may use Fortune and conditions to keep this damage from taking them out, per usual. Characters using the juice can take a degree of fatigue to mitigate damage before having to take injured and wounded conditions. For long-term acceleration during an interlude, the GM may ask for a Constitution (Stamina) test, with the result determining the characters’ condition at the end of the trip, or simply choose to assign a degree of fatigue to the characters to reflect the arduous nature of their travel.

Crowds

While encounters with a small group of NPCs are handled through combat or social tests, an angry or panicked crowd presents a separate hazard, where the rush of people becomes like a force of nature. This can be especially dangerous in a confined space, such as a station airlock. Characters facing a dangerous crowd must make a Strength (Might) or Willpower (Courage) test to avoid being swept into it, ranging from TN 11 to 15 depending on the crowd size. A failed test requires a subsequent Constitution (Stamina) test to avoid 1d6 damage from being shoved or trampled. Characters can repeat these tests each round to escape the crowd or avoid further damage. They might also make a Communication test to sway or calm the crowd, applying an appropriate focus at the GM’s discretion.

Environmental Exposure

Humans have a narrow range of comfortable temperatures, which environmental systems on ships and stations work hard to maintain. Prolonged exposure to an inhospitable environment presents a clear hazard. These environments can be found on worlds across the Sol system; in addition, every alien world presents an environment humans are not adapted for. This might be an atmosphere choked with heavy dust or grit, for example, or the too-bright light of a red giant sun. To resist the effects of exposure, characters must make periodic Constitution (Stamina) tests, starting at TN 9 with the difficulty escalating +1 per additional test. How often this test is required depends on the intensity of the exposure, ranging from every hour to every minute for intense, terrestrial environments. A failed test results in 1d6 damage. A character can take a degree of fatigue in place of damage. Any character taken out by damage is unconscious and any further damage results in a dying condition. Exposure to Vacuum is a particular hazard, described later in this section.

Geologic Or Weather Event

Not every planet in the gate network is entirely stable—nor is Earth, at times—and a fledgling colony is at risk from any extreme weather their new home throws at them. Characters can make a challenge test to find appropriate cover from one of these events, at the GM’s discretion; for example, a Constitution (Running) test to reach shelter or a Perception (Survival) test to spot an item or safe location. Characters without cover or protection must make a Constitution (Stamina) test to avoid taking damage. The Hazard Category should be based on the severity of the event; for example, remaining upright during a minor tremor would be minor, but navigating a rockslide would be major or arduous. A prolonged event might require periodic tests with changing difficulties to reflect the event worsening or subsiding.

Illness

Characters may be exposed to a variety of bacteria, viruses, or pathogens that cause illness; this becomes exponentially more likely on alien worlds, either from alien organics or a spoiled food supply. To avoid infection, an exposed character must make a Constitution (Tolerance) test with a TN based on the virulence of the disease, ranging from TN 7 (touch contact from someone with a cold) to TN 15 (direct exposure to a designer virus). Generally, the course of an illness is a challenge test requiring further Constitution (Tolerance) tests, with the potential for Intelligence (Medicine) tests to add to the success threshold. The interval for these tests is based on the illness’s progression, anywhere from a day or so to a few hours. Consequences of a failed test and the progression of an illness can include difficulty on further tests or developing advanced symptoms in the form of conditions, such as Blind or Hindered. For a deadly disease, the major consequence is the character acquiring the dying condition. When exposed to bacteria, viruses or pathogens from alien worlds, you may choose to increase the test difficulty to reflect the character’s lack of immunity.

Impact

Falling in an environment with variable or microgravity is often more an issue of impact. As they say, it’s not the fall, it’s the sudden stop (or change in inertia) that hurts. An impact equivalent to a short fall (3 to 4 meters) in 1 g is around 2d6 damage, while longer falls do more damage, up to 6d6. In some situations, characters can make a Dexterity (Acrobatics) test to halve the damage from an impact by rolling with it and landing to absorb some of the shock. Some “impacts” result from sudden changes in acceleration, throwing characters hard against the bulkheads of ships or stations. Generally, acceleration couches mitigate this (although see Acceleration, previously) but someone who isn’t strapped in when a ship suddenly accelerates, decelerates, or maneuvers can suffer damage equivalent to a serious fall.

Radiation

Radiation presents a higher danger on a ship or station, where radiation shielding can fail or a character might encounter an experiment without proper protection. A planet’s atmosphere or the intensity of its star might also make radiation more of a hazard than on Earth. Depending on the type of radiation and its concentration, a character may not notice the effects for hours or days after exposure—or within seconds, such as a fatal gamma-ray burst.

The most common form of this hazard is acute radiation syndrome, or radiation sickness, which is caused by exposure to any radiation that breaks down the human body’s molecular structure—for example, gamma. Symptoms include nausea, bleeding, and hair loss. Like with Illness, characters must make a Constitution (Tolerance) test to resist the effects of radiation sickness— essentially toughing out the symptoms. Characters failing this test immediately acquire a degree of fatigue; each additional failed test results in another degree of fatigue, followed by acquiring the blinded or defenseless condition. Unlike Illness, there is no challenge test to resist or avoid radiation exposure. Only proper protective equipment will shield a character. Medical treatment for radiation comes in a variety of forms; decontamination is FuSANG SEEdPOdSeffective against external exposure, while more advanced treatments, such as proteins that promote white blood cell growth, can repair internal damage. This can include unexpected emotional reactions, altered perception, memory loss and more—typically something specific and sometimes difficult to predict. Characters must make a Willpower (Self- Discipline) test to resist the effect of one of these structures or artifacts; the Target Number should start at TN 9 to 13 depending on the intensity of the effect, increasing by +1 for each subsequent test. Failing this test applies an appropriate condition, which can be removed either through time, a repeated test, or distance from the structure or artifact.

Starvation and Dehydration

Humans can go without water for a day. After this, a TN 9 Constitution (Stamina) test is required to avoid acquiring a degree of fatigue. An additional test is required for each hour without water, increasing the TN by +1 per test. Each subsequent failed test increases the degree of fatigue, followed by the unconscious and then dying conditions, unless the character gets water. Likewise, a character can go without food for 3 days, after which they must make the same test as for dehydration, except additional tests are once per day. The character cannot recover from the acquired conditions until they receive the necessary nutrition and hydration.

Suffocation

In the absence of breathable air, characters can hold their breath for a number of rounds equal to twice their Constitution score. After that, they must make a TN 9 Constitution (Stamina) test each round, with the TN increasing by +1 per round, to continue holding their breath. Failing the test renders the character unconscious. On the following round, the character’s condition becomes dying, and the character cannot stabilize until they are able to breathe again. A character stabilized from dying due to suffocation is exhausted.

Toxic Atmosphere

While humans can survive in atmospheres slightly different from Earth’s, there is a certain threshold at which an alien atmosphere becomes dangerous—too much oxygen or nitrogen, for example, or high concentrations of toxic elements like chlorine or sulfur. For a toxic atmosphere, follow the same approach as described for Environmental Exposure, noting whether the atmosphere’s elements make it difficult to breathe or might also irritate or damage the skin, eyes or internal organs. Protective equipment or an Intelligence (Science) test can increase the success threshold for tests related to toxic atmosphere.

Toxic Gas Emissions

Venturing into underground caverns or across rocky plains isn’t only risky because of potential cave-ins or rockslides. The same sorts of toxic chemicals that create a choking atmosphere can issue from vents or similar cracks in the ground, sometimes with little to no warning. A character within close range of a vent when it erupts must make a TN 13 Dexterity (Acrobatics) test or take 4d6 damage. The specific gas or substance—a corrosive acid, for example— may also inflict a condition. In the case of a location where gas is continually rising from an open vent, refer to the rules for Environmental Exposure.

Toxins

A variety of substances can prove toxic to humans, both within the Sol system and on alien worlds. Toxins can be directly injected into the human body, for instance through an animal bite, or a character might be exposed through ingestion, inhalation, or skin contact. The same approach as Illness can be taken with toxins, including the higher test difficulty for alien toxins. Note that for some toxins, characters might only be able to achieve the success threshold for stabilization with medical assistance, such as receiving an antivenom. Otherwise, it’s simply a matter of time before the character suffers the worst consequences of the hazard.

Vacuum

Exposure to the vacuum of space is a constant danger and almost always fatal. On the round following exposure to vacuum, the character’s condition becomes dying. The character additionally suffers 6d6 damage at the start of each round of exposure to the cold and radiation of space. A TN 15 Constitution (Tolerance) test halves this damage. A character taken out by vacuum exposure damage is immediately dead. Generally, either Constitution loss or damage will kill the character quickly, although there is a slight chance of survival if they are brought into a safe environment before either of those things occurs and their dying condition is stabilized.

In addition to the antagonists, complications, and other threats characters face in The Expanse, one hazard deserves special attention: the protomolecule.

Origins

The protomolecule is an extra-terrestrial particle first discovered on Phoebe by the Martian Congressional Republic. The corporation Protogen discovered its ability to infect and radically alter life forms to repurpose their biology for its own objectives—but designed by the ring builders as a tool, not a weapon. Even so, Protogen’s initial experiments with the protomolecule proved disastrous, including the deliberate infection of Eros Station and the deadly Project Caliban hybrids. After the creation of the Sol Ring, humanity discovered that protomolecule had been used to build structures on countless alien worlds, such as Ilus. The last known protomolecule sample in the Sol system, meanwhile, was stolen by the Free Navy and given to Winston Duarte.

Protomolecule Effects

  • Within the Sol system, it is incredibly unlikely to encounter a sample of protomolecule, especially during the Transport Union era. However, the use of protomolecule to shape worlds in the ring network offers more risk of contact on alien worlds. If you choose to use the protomolecule in your campaign, the following rules are recommended:
  • The protomolecule only affects biological life and only by direct contact.
  • It is anaerobic and cannot be transmitted through the air.
  • Any character who comes into contact with the protomolecule must make a TN 18 Constitution (Tolerance) test or become immediately infected.

Once the character is infected, the GM rolls 2d6 and adds the character’s Constitution. This becomes the number of days the character has before they are overcome by the effects of the protomolecule. In the event they are exposed to high levels of radiation, the time to total infection changes to hours instead of days.

Protomolecule Infection Symptoms

The symptoms of the protomolecule begin like those of a mild cold, quickly transforming into something like a violent fever. The character becomes increasingly disoriented and fatigued. As the infection spreads, brown fluid leaks from their orifices until the victim is completely debilitated. The victim begins to hallucinate and may require Willpower (Self-Discipline) tests to focus on anything or avoid random outbursts of emotion (usually rage or sadness). After half the infection time, dark splotchy brown and black marks spread across the skin, and the character begins to stagger about uncontrollably, vomiting infectious brown fluid at other life forms. At this point, the victim is no longer a Player Character, but under the control of the protomolecule; they become an NPC controlled by the GM (see vomit zombie under Adversaries).

Every corner of the world of The Expanse hides dangerous figures. This section contains a starting selection of adversaries for your campaign, such as opportunistic pirates looking for a score, government officials pushing an agenda, and alien lifeforms found through the ring gates. In addition, this section provides guidelines on creating your own adversaries or strengthening the NPCs provided here.

Statistics Format

Adversaries are presented in a common format: a description combined with game statistics, sometimes referred to as a “stat block.” If you’ve read this far into the book, the stats should be fairly self-explanatory. Note that each adversary has an entry for favored stunts. These are provided as a suggestion; as always, use your best judgment. An adversary can use any basic stunt permitted by the Game Master.

Adversary Training

Unless otherwise noted in their description, adversaries are considered trained in all the weapons they carry, and in any other attacks calculated for them in their game statistics. Similarly, adversaries wearing armor are trained in its use. The Game Master decides which, if any, other weapons and armor any adversary is trained in.

Thus, thugs are assumed to appear in a group roughly equal to the size of a party of PCs, while a bounty hunter might strike the party solo. As always, GMs should be aware of the PCs’ individual capabilities and any significant things that might make them more or less effective against a particular adversary. A larger than normal group, special knowledge of an adversary, and numerous other factors can cause the actual Threat to shift from its baseline. Armor Rating (AR) can be especially difficult for PCs to deal with at low levels; in general, you likely do not want a foe to have an AR higher than the PCs’ average level, regardless of what a stat block says.

The More Threatening Adversary

The adversaries presented in this section represent the average for that type and often make effective opponents in groups or supporting more significant NPCs. Sometimes, throwing a twist on a familiar adversary increases an encounter’s tension. Perhaps the sergeant in a Martian squad was trained differently than their peers; a veteran smuggler has tricks the rest of the crew don’t know. From a mechanics perspective, making a more threatening adversary can involve modifying weapons or armor to create different tactical challenges, or modifying their stats. The changes can be as varied as you like, but the following guidelines are a useful starting point.

Elite

Elites are a little tougher than average, bumping them one Threat Level higher than other adversaries of the same type. These are your veterans, senior professionals, and dominant social players.

ABILITIES: Add 1 to any three abilities FOCUSES: Add two FORTUNE: Add 8 + (Constitution × 2) QUALITIES (OPTIONAL): Make the NPC a Novice in a new talent or add a degree to an existing one

Heroic

A heroic adversary is exceptional. They benefit from a mixture of talent and experience that often leads to a reputation as the best in their region—the hero of their own story, in a way. Officers with a high rank, infamous ship captains or crew, or noted experts could be heroic adversaries.

ABILITIES: Add 2 to any two abilities and 1 to any three others FOCUSES: Add four FORTUNE: Add 16 + (Constitution × 4) QUALITIES (OPTIONAL): Make the NPC a Novice in two new talents or add two degrees to existing ones

Epic

Epic adversaries represent the most serious threat to the Player Characters and possess the highest degree of personal power. Someone who commands the authority of an entire station, has achieved one of the highest positions in a hierarchy, or wields inhuman abilities can be an epic adversary with the strength of a primary antagonist.

ABILITIES: Add 3 to one ability, 2 to any two other abilities, and 1 to any three others FOCUSES: Add six TOUGHNESS: Increase Armor Rating by 3 FORTUNE: Add 24 + (Constitution × 6) QUALITIES (OPTIONAL): Add the equivalent of three degrees to new or existing talents

Zeroes

Most NPCs in The Expanse are Zeroes. This does not make them inferior to other characters; they still live rich, dramatic lives. Zeroes simply don’t interact with the rules and story of the game beyond the basic function of everyday people, such as informants, clerks, passersby on a station, or the victims of an alien weapon. This includes non-combatants seeking cover during a combat encounter. Zeroes use the same stat block, presented here.

Supporting Cast

Some supporting characters the heroes encounter are friendly, passive, or simply bystanders not looking for a fight. These NPCs do not require full stat blocks, as they appear only for a handful of roleplaying encounters. Instead, an abbreviated stat block illustrates a supporting character’s abilities and focuses, sufficient for a background NPC who receives occasional interaction. This abbreviated stat block is also useful for social adversaries who aren’t expected to fight the characters. Note that every supporting character also has the Optional Potential quality described for Zeroes. Here are a few examples of supporting characters:

Arjo Dimas Entrepreneur

Did you know you can compress certain Martian silicate into glass? Arjo figured this out first and now he’s selling unique statuettes from a small shop in Syria Plantum. This puts him on a first-name basis with customers from the government and MCRN, some of whom like to gossip.

Cassidy Cooker “deckhand”

Technically, Cassidy snuck aboard the Union freighter Glimpse the Horizon and refused to leave. But the crew took a shine to the kid and didn’t feel right being the next to abandon her, so now she’s de facto crew. Characters brought aboard Glimpse the Horizon either win over an ally or deal with a nuisance who knows they mean trouble.

Ohemaa Gbeho Journalist

On the hunt for her first major break, Ohemaa is a junior reporter away from Earth for the first time. All she needs is to get over her queasiness whenever she’s in zero-g and she can bring her quirky, excitable reporting attitude to bear.

Tong Liu Ambassador’s Assistant

Every ambassador sent to treat with the Transport Union needs staff, and Tong takes pride in their role— even though they’re the only one who volunteered from their fledgling colony. They keep their ambassador’s life very organized on Medina Station and witness plenty of goings-on, making
